title: Intelligence as a Non-Saturating Economic Substrate: Inference, Satiety, and Capital Stewardship

detail.title: Intelligence as a Non-Saturating Economic Substrate: Inference, Satiety, and Capital Stewardship
detail.abstract: Economic history suggests that every category of output-from agricultural goods to manufactured products, consumer software, and network services-eventually reaches a point at which additional supply saturates demand and compresses prices. This regularity underpins much of modern intuition about value, competition, and capital allocation. This paper advances a simple but asymmetric claim: if intelligence, realized at the point of inference, behaves not as a saturating consumer good but as a non-saturating, recursively generative input, then the logic of satiety fails at the margin where intelligence operates. Under that condition, expanding the supply of intelligence does not extinguish demand; it creates new demand by enabling new problems, new tasks, and new transformations. No prescriptive recommendations are offered. Instead, the paper provides a structural lens. Readers who recognize the asymmetry between saturating goods and nonsaturating intelligence may infer, over time, which forms of investment remain coherent in a world where value scales with capability rather than with scarcity.

title: Patrolling the Securities Laws: Toward the SEC's Investigation of Founder-CEO Firms
affiliations: California State University, Fullerton - Department of Finance, University of Missouri at Columbia - Robert J. Trulaske, Sr. College of Business and Clark University - Graduate School of Management

detail.title: Patrolling the Securities Laws: Toward the SEC's Investigation of Founder-CEO Firms
detail.abstract: Using hand-collected data on founder CEOs and SEC investigations obtained through Freedom of Information Act requests, we find that firms led by founder-CEO are 29% more likely to face SEC investigations, though these investigations rarely lead to accounting and auditing enforcement release actions. CEO attributes—power, risk-taking, and visibility—drive this heightened attention, consistent with the SEC's broad strategy that seeks to hold individuals accountable. Investors of founder-led firms appear compensated for the increased investigation risk through superior stock performance. Overall, our findings on the regulatory consequences of founder CEOs provide direct evidence of SEC's strategic emphasis on individual accountability.

detail.title: The Information Economics of Green Transitions
detail.abstract: Economics traditionally explain environmental market failures through the lens of exter nalities. This paper shows that the failure could be significantly driven by a "lemons" problem. While environmental concerns have been rapidly rising among consumers, many key attributes (emissions, production processes) are unobservable to consumers and only disclosed voluntarily by firms. The evidence shows that voluntary disclosure enables brown firms to greenwash consumers. We develop a simple framework to incorporate information into the analysis of green transitions. We microfound greenwashing in a voluntary disclosure model and embed the friction into models of green markets and technical change to study positive and normative implications. Greenwashing creates a "lemons" problem that unravels green production and R&D, even when consumers are environmentally con scious. Mandatory environmental disclosure accelerates the green transition and makes Pigouvian instruments more effective. Evidence suggests that its effects could parallel those of large carbon taxes.

title: Do Audited Financial Reports Mitigate (or Exacerbate) Stock Market Crashes?
affiliations: Vanderbilt University - Owen Graduate School of Management and Duke University - Fuqua School of Business

detail.title: Do Audited Financial Reports Mitigate (or Exacerbate) Stock Market Crashes?
detail.abstract: Does audit assurance mitigate stock market crashes? We find this is not the case, contrary to conventional wisdom. Building on confirmation bias theory, we predict that audited financial statements may give investors a false sense of security regarding the firm's fundamental value, potentially amplifying bubbles and crashes. To test this prediction, we compare stock price changes of firms with and without external audits around the Wall Street Crash of 1929––an important event that motivated the audit mandate in the Securities Act of 1934. Diverging from prevailing belief, we find that audited firms experienced more severe price declines than unaudited firms. Further analyses reveal larger bubbles for audited firms relative to unaudited firms, as reflected in both higher stock prices and valuation multiples, supporting the confirmation bias view. Our evidence has important implications for audit regulation in many emerging disclosure areas, such as crowdfunding, cryptocurrencies, and ESG disclosures.

title: Beneficial Ownership: The New Tax Anti-Evasion Test in Indian Customs Law

detail.title: Beneficial Ownership: The New Tax Anti-Evasion Test in Indian Customs Law
detail.abstract: Indian laws are progressively adopting anti tax avoidance rules. By way of a recent amendment, the Indian customs law framework has adopted the 'beneficial owner' test. While the contours of this test are well known, it has been adopted with certain variation. It brings within the purview of the Indian customs law (a) any person on whose behalf the goods are being imported or exported; and (b) any person who exercises effective control over the goods being imported or exported. Recently the Customs Tribunal approved the application of the test to hold the ultimate beneficiary of goods manufactured by third-party importers are the real importer. In this wake, this article explores the contours of the 'beneficial owner' test in the Indian customs law framework and its implications.

title: Ideological Bias and Breach of the Fiduciary Duty of Care
affiliations: University of Southern California - Marshall School of Business

detail.title: Ideological Bias and Breach of the Fiduciary Duty of Care
detail.abstract: This paper analyzes a remedy for breach of the fiduciary duty of care in a principal-advisor relationship. The advisor's effort cost is ideologically too high for a certain investment. This bias can lead to a breach of care, if the advisor's investigative effort is unobservable by the principal. The principal audits and sues the agent, if there is a signal indicating a breach. We show that this process does not lead to efficiency. To correct this problem we offer a mechanism which can implement efficiency. The (active) court precommits to a function whose image value scales expectation damages and depends on the degree of bias of the agent and a minimum audit probability. The damage scale factor may inflate or deflate expectation damages. We consider cases where the principal is risk neutral and risk averse.

title: Risk Preferences in Political Campaigns: Effects on Voter Trust

detail.title: Risk Preferences in Political Campaigns: Effects on Voter Trust
detail.abstract: Voter trust in democracies is declining, yet existing accounts struggle to explain why politicians systematically adopt risk-seeking or overly cautious strategies that alienate the electorate. This paper argues that a key mechanism driving this erosion is a risk preference channel shaped by institutional thresholds. I develop a simple formal model showing that politicians facing discrete political rewards, such as winning an election or securing a party nomination, optimally switch between risk-seeking and risk-aversion based on their position relative to these thresholds. This survival-oriented calculus systematically misaligns their actions with the risk preferences of the median voter, leading to policy distortion and perceived inconsistency that corrodes long-term trust. The theory is tested through structured process tracing of strategic episodes in Germany, the United States, and South Korea. The empirical evidence confirms the predicted polarity of risk behavior and indicates that electoral systems moderate its intensity. The findings reframe a root cause of democratic distrust as an institutional incentive problem, suggesting that reforms targeting the design of political thresholds can help preserve public trust.

title: Constructing Model-based Cross-Section Factors in the Corporate Bond Market
affiliations: Fudan University - School of Management and Shanghai Jiao Tong University (SJTU) - Shanghai Advanced Institute of Finance (SAIF)

detail.title: Constructing Model-based Cross-Section Factors in the Corporate Bond Market
detail.abstract: Using a structural model of default with stochastic interest rates and liquidity shocks, we extract three common risk factors-credit, duration, and liquidity-from the crosssection of corporate bond returns. Our estimation is unique in that, instead of bond characteristics, we use the model-implied factor loadings of bond returns on the three state variables of the model-the systematic asset value, interest rate and liquidity. Our theory-based three-factor model can explain corporate bond risk premiums in both the aggregate and cross-section. Moreover, the model-implied factors can be used to gauge the relative importance of credit, liquidity, and duration, allowing us to identify distinct episodes of flights-to-quality, flights-to-liquidity and flights-to-cash. We further demonstrate the broader implications of the factors: the credit factor explains stock and sovereign returns, the liquidity factor reflects dealers' post-regulation capacity, and the duration factor measures the convenience yield of US Treasuries.

title: From No-Tail Microeconomic Shocks to Heavy-Tail Macroeconomic Outcomes: A Network-Based Theory of Disaster Risk
affiliations: and University of Illinois at Urbana-Champaign

detail.title: From No-Tail Microeconomic Shocks to Heavy-Tail Macroeconomic Outcomes: A Network-Based Theory of Disaster Risk
detail.abstract: This paper examines the microfoundation of macroeconomic tail risk, defined as the frequency of extremely negative GDP downturns relative to what is predicted by a normal distribution. We demonstrate that firm-level productivity shocks, even when normally distributed, can be amplified into large macroeconomic tail events through a dynamic production-based inputoutput network, challenging the traditional view that only sufficiently large firm-level shocks impact the aggregate market. The evolving network structure, driven by technological shocks, hinders risk diversification across firms, delays the mean reversion of aggregate volatility, and causes volatility to cluster from local to global scales over time. In bad times, when idiosyncratic risks are high and firms treat all inputs as complementary, these risk spillovers can accumulate, resulting in severe GDP downturns.

title: Social Media are a Threat for Democracy! – A Political Perspective for Analyzing and Diminishing Harm
affiliations: Copenhagen Business School, IULM University, University of Zurich - IBW Department of Business Administration and Leuphana University of Lueneburg - Institute of Business Administration

detail.title: Social Media are a Threat for Democracy! – A Political Perspective for Analyzing and Diminishing Harm
detail.abstract: Social media platforms, once hailed as potential champions of dialogue, have evolved into commodified spaces in which their business models incentivize hate speech, misinformation, polarization, and the political fragmentation of society, benefiting corporate and political elites while eroding democracy. The existing market and technological conceptualizations of social media platforms offer only partial analysis of and solutions to these issues. This paper advances a political perspective grounded in deliberative democracy, arguing that social media companies are political actors responsible for maintaining a well-functioning public sphere. We argue that transforming social media platforms into true facilitators of democratic discourse requires enhancing their deliberative capacity. Beyond the capacities of the public sphere suggested by the market and technology perspectives (1) transparency and accountability and (2) openness and inclusiveness; we propose that fostering deliberative capacity also requires (3) conduciveness to argumentation and (4) consequentiality. We thus contribute to understanding how management theories can explain and address current threats to democracy.

title: AI Boom: Analysing the Austrian School's Economic Ideas

detail.title: AI Boom: Analysing the Austrian School's Economic Ideas
detail.abstract: The swift growth of artificial intelligence technologies has instigated significant structural transformations in global markets, leading to a resurgence of interest in theoretical frameworks that elucidate entrepreneurial discovery, capital reallocation, and innovation cycles. This article examines the current AI boom using the economic theories of the Austrian School, referencing the contributions of Mises, Hayek, Kirzner, and Schumpeter. It contends that the AI surge exhibits decentralised knowledge processes, wherein entrepreneurial entities assess fragmented information and vie to predict unpredictable future wants. The research examines the emergence of malinvestment hazards due to misleading pricing signals in exuberant investment environments, alongside the capacity of spontaneous market adjustments to reallocate resources towards sustainable applications. By using Austrian ideas like subjective value, capital heterogeneity, and entrepreneurial awareness, the research gives us a way to think about both the creative energy and possible weaknesses of the AI revolution that is happening right now. The research finds that an Austrian viewpoint provides significant understanding of the catalysts, trends, and enduring consequences of AI-fueled economic change.

title: The Constitution of India and its Linkages with Intellectual Property Rights

detail.title: The Constitution of India and its Linkages with Intellectual Property Rights
detail.abstract: India's intellectual property rights regime operates without an explicit constitutional clause on intellectual property. Instead, its foundation rests on a combination of legislative competence rules, property jurisprudence, fundamental rights, treatyimplementation powers, and continuity provisions. This paper analyzes how the Constitution shapes the scope and evolution of Indian intellectual property law. It also situates biodiversity, plant varieties, and traditional knowledge within the constitutional framework. The analysis shows that the Constitution provides a flexible structure that supports a balanced and socially responsive IP system. The study concludes by highlighting challenges emerging from digital technologies and knowledge-intensive sectors.

title: The Morning After: Late-night TV and the Stock Market
affiliations: , Cardiff Business School, University of Cambridge and Cardiff University - Cardiff Business School

detail.title: The Morning After: Late-night TV and the Stock Market
detail.abstract: Binge-watching late-night TV shows has become far more common due to the popularity of streaming services such as Netflix and Amazon and their 'dump release' of new shows at midnight. We examine how the sleep loss associated with this phenomenon affects financial markets and find that market returns significantly decline on the day following the release of popular late-night shows. This effect is stronger in stocks with larger market-cap, and higher price. We show that sleepdeprived investors are less willing to make buying decisions since they require larger cognitive effort compared to selling decisions. Instead, they make more heuristicdriven sales, causing a decline in market returns. We also show that this proxy for sleep loss is superior to the one traditionally used in the literature, i.e., Daylight Savings Time change. Our findings are not driven by noise traders and are robust to a wide range of alternative explanations.

title: AI Governance after MiFID II: Beyond (Mere) Technological Neutrality?
affiliations: University of Glasgow - School of Law

detail.title: AI Governance after MiFID II: Beyond (Mere) Technological Neutrality?
detail.abstract: This article examines the evolving intersections between Artificial Intelligence (AI) and EU financial regulation, focusing on the Markets in Financial Instruments Directive II (MiFID II). Grounded in the principle of technological neutrality, MiFID II seeks to enhance investor protection, safeguard market integrity, and ensure that innovation develops within competitive and well-regulated markets across the Union. The article argues, however, that while this neutrality renders the framework functionally enabling, it also leaves it normatively silent in the face of the distinctive and evolving risks introduced by financial AI. As AI applications become increasingly heterogeneous-both in the financial functions in which they are deployed and in their underlying AI lifecycles and value chains-MiFID II's activity-based logic shows growing difficulty in accommodating their diverse and evolving risk profiles. Reflecting the EU's broader shift toward risk-based AI governance, the article outlines an initial taxonomy intended to guide a proportionate alignment of regulatory obligations with AI-related risks, thereby supporting the continued adaptability, coherence, and future-proofing of EU financial services regulation.

title: A Typology of Socially Responsible Public Procurement(SRPP)

detail.title: A Typology of Socially Responsible Public Procurement(SRPP)
detail.abstract: Background and Aim: Social responsibility is an emergent concern within public procurement, one that has wide-ranging implications for stakeholders at the micro (supply chain) and meso (society) levels. This chapter classifies the different types of socially responsible public procurement (SRPP), leading to a proposed new typology and definition. Research Design and Methods: The chapter undertakes a narrative review to investigate SRPP. This involves searching for academic and "grey" literature using a combination of systematic and snowballing strategies, and subsequently synthesising the output to create a typology of SRPP. Findings: Three main SRPP types are identified. The first is to do with employment (creating job opportunities, upholding labour standards, tackling human rights abuses). The second is to do with entrepreneurship (supporting third-sector enterprises, operating preference programmes, treating suppliers fairly, buying local). The third is to do with service quality (making public services accessible, delivering quality public services). Research Limitations: The typology is unlikely to be exhaustive of all SRPP types. It also requires empirical validation from experienced practitioners through a Delphi-type study. Theoretical Contribution: The typology identifies the core dimensions of SRPP and proposes a new definition of the SRPP concept. Both can be used as the basis for future empirical and conceptual inquiry. Contribution to UN SDGs: The chapter explains how SRPP exemplifies UN SDG #12, Sustainable Consumption & Production and complements UN SDG #8 Decent Work and UN SDG #9 Industry. Practical impact: The typology educates practitioners about the various ways in which public procurement can be managed to achieve social value outcomes.

title: Credit-Market Sentiment: Estimation and Macroeconomic Implications
affiliations: Federal Reserve Bank of Boston, Banco de España, Federal Reserve Banks - Federal Reserve Bank of Richmond, Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System and Federal Reserve Bank of Boston

detail.title: Credit-Market Sentiment: Estimation and Macroeconomic Implications
detail.abstract: We lay out a signal-extraction statistical model to estimate a factor summarizing conditions in U.S. credit markets. The factor provides a real-time gauge of "sentiment" in credit markets, above and beyond that attributable to contemporaneous economic conditions. Fluctuations in the credit-market sentiment factor have strong asymmetric and nonlinear effects on economic activity, depending not only on the sign and magnitude of the credit market sentiment shock, but also on the current state of the economy. A positive credit-market sentiment shock has a stronger and more persistent effect on real economic activity at the onset of a crisis than amidst an expansionary period. Instead, negative sentiment shocks have more persistent effects on activity during expansions than in recessions. Our credit-market sentiment measure is a robust predictor of aggregate credit dynamics that outperforms financial indicators in the literature, and correlates positively with forecast errors of quarterly corporate earnings growth one quarter ahead. Finally, our results indicate that tightening (easing) monetary policy shocks temporarily deteriorate (improve) credit market sentiment. Our findings suggest that monetary policy "leans against the wind" of credit market overheating, and highlight that easy unanticipated monetary policy should be taken into account by policymakers, as it might contribute to the build-up of credit market vulnerabilities.
